scenes.visual: Title card 'Where the Sunshine Goes' fades in over a beach: TAN sand on the left, pale BLUE water on the right, one sun above both. Same world and colour map as the first film. THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures. Each water molecule is a wide V-shaped block: a large body block for oxygen at the point and two small tip blocks for the hydrogens. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene, in both films and in the lesson's figures: OXYGEN END = RED, labelled 'slightly negative' (δ−); HYDROGEN ENDS = BLUE, labelled 'slightly positive' (δ+); COVALENT BOND inside a molecule = short solid GREY bar; HYDROGEN BOND between molecules = dashed GOLD line; liquid WATER as a substance = pale BLUE fill; SAND = TAN; ENERGY = small ORANGE dots; OIL = pale GREEN droplet; CELLULOSE fibre = light BROWN strand. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Same sun, same afternoon. Why is the beach sand too hot to stand on, while the water beside it still feels cool? The first film showed water molecules tugging on each other through hydrogen bonds. Now we follow the sunshine's energy into that web.
scenes.visual: The sun sends identical ORANGE energy dots down onto both the TAN sand and the BLUE water. A bare foot hops off the sand; a hand rests in the water. A question mark. A small inset of the first film's crowd of V molecules with flickering dashed GOLD lines slides into the corner.
scenes.narration: Same sun, same afternoon. Why is the beach sand too hot to stand on, while the water beside it still feels cool? The first film showed water molecules tugging on each other through hydrogen bonds. Now we follow the sunshine's energy into that web.

scenes.tts: First, what does a thermometer read? Temperature tracks the average energy of motion of a substance's particles. Faster jiggling means a higher temperature, and slower jiggling means a lower one.
scenes.visual: A thermometer stands beside a box of small dots. As the dots jiggle faster, the thermometer's column rises; as they slow, it falls. Label: 'temperature reflects average energy of motion (kinetic energy) of particles'.
scenes.narration: First, what does a thermometer read? Temperature tracks the average energy of motion of a substance's particles. Faster jiggling means a higher temperature, and slower jiggling means a lower one.

scenes.tts: Take equal masses of dry sand and water, side by side. Give each exactly the same amount of energy. Then watch where that energy goes.
scenes.visual: Two equal blocks slide in: TAN 'dry sand, 100 g' and BLUE 'water, 100 g', each with a thermometer. Above each, an identical meter fills with ORANGE dots to the same mark, labelled '836.8 J each'.
scenes.narration: Take equal masses of dry sand and water, side by side. Give each exactly the same amount of energy. Then watch where that energy goes.

scenes.tts: In the sand, the particles vibrate harder, and the pulls between them stretch a little. Its thermometer climbs about ten degrees.
scenes.visual: All the ORANGE dots pour into one energy meter on the TAN block. Every particle shakes harder, and the thin springs drawn between neighbouring particles stretch slightly at the same time. The sand thermometer climbs; a tag shows 'about +10 °C'. Label 'one energy account: faster vibration + stretched attractions'. Corner label 'schematic'. On-screen arithmetic, not spoken: '836.8 ÷ (100 × 0.8) ≈ 10.5 °C'.
scenes.narration: In the sand, the particles vibrate harder, and the pulls between them stretch a little. Its thermometer climbs about ten degrees.

scenes.tts: In the water, the molecules speed up too. But the web of hydrogen bonds also stretches, bends and rearranges, and that takes extra energy. So each degree costs water more, and its thermometer climbs only about two degrees.
scenes.visual: All the ORANGE dots pour into one energy meter on the BLUE block, the same amount as the sand's. Molecules shake harder while, at the same time, dashed GOLD lines stretch, bend, snap and re-form with new partners. No dot is drawn going to only motion or only bonds. Label 'one energy account: faster motion + rearranging hydrogen-bond web'. The water thermometer climbs a little; tag 'about +2 °C'. Corner label 'schematic'. On screen, not spoken: '836.8 ÷ (100 × 4.18) = 2.0 °C'.
scenes.narration: In the water, the molecules speed up too. But the web of hydrogen bonds also stretches, bends and rearranges, and that takes extra energy. So each degree costs water more, and its thermometer climbs only about two degrees.

scenes.tts: This is specific heat, the energy needed to warm one gram by one degree. Per gram, water needs about five times as much energy as dry sand. Its specific heat is high.
scenes.visual: Two bars, labelled 'specific heat (J per g per °C)': TAN 'dry sand ≈ 0.8' and BLUE 'water ≈ 4.18', the blue bar about five times taller. A small label 'per gram'.
scenes.narration: This is specific heat, the energy needed to warm one gram by one degree. Per gram, water needs about five times as much energy as dry sand. Its specific heat is high.

scenes.tts: Night falls, and both blocks cool. Say each loses energy at the same steady rate. Will the water's temperature fall faster or slower than the sand's? Pause and decide.
scenes.visual: The sun sets; the sky darkens. Both blocks sit warm, thermometers high. Identical small streams of ORANGE dots leave each block at the same rate, labelled 'same energy loss per minute'. A question mark between the blocks.
scenes.narration: Night falls, and both blocks cool. Say each loses energy at the same steady rate. Will the water's temperature fall faster or slower than the sand's? Pause and decide.

scenes.visual: Hold the night scene. A small 5-second countdown ring empties in the corner.

scenes.tts: Slower. Each degree of cooling must release about five times as much energy from the water. As its hydrogen bonds re-form, they give energy back. So the water stays warm longer, while the sand cools quickly.
scenes.visual: Equal streams of ORANGE dots keep leaving both blocks. GOLD dashes snap back on in the BLUE block, each releasing a small ORANGE dot; the water thermometer sinks slowly. The TAN thermometer drops fast. Labels 'same energy loss per minute' and 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Slower. Each degree of cooling must release about five times as much energy from the water. As its hydrogen bonds re-form, they give energy back. So the water stays warm longer, while the sand cools quickly.

scenes.tts: But a bay is not one gram. Heat capacity is the energy needed to warm a whole object by one degree. For one substance, it is the mass times the specific heat. A cup and a bathtub of water share the same specific heat. Yet the bathtub has far more heat capacity. Under the same heater, it warms far more slowly.
scenes.visual: A cup of BLUE water and a bathtub of BLUE water sit under identical heat lamps, receiving the same stream of ORANGE dots. In the cup the dots crowd together and its thermometer rises; in the bathtub the same dots spread thin and its thermometer barely moves. Label 'heat capacity = mass × specific heat'.
scenes.narration: But a bay is not one gram. Heat capacity is the energy needed to warm a whole object by one degree. For one substance, it is the mass times the specific heat. A cup and a bathtub of water share the same specific heat. Yet the bathtub has far more heat capacity. Under the same heater, it warms far more slowly.

scenes.tts: Now picture the Bay. Waves and currents mix the warm surface water downward. So the day's sunshine spreads through a huge mass of water. Some energy also leaves the surface, as water evaporates.
scenes.visual: Zoom out from the bathtub to a wide cross-section of the Bay. ORANGE dots fall on the top layer, then curling wave arrows carry them down into deeper BLUE layers, spreading them out. At the surface a few dots rise away as wisps of vapour, labelled 'evaporation'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Now picture the Bay. Waves and currents mix the warm surface water downward. So the day's sunshine spreads through a huge mass of water. Some energy also leaves the surface, as water evaporates.

scenes.tts: So three things keep a bay steady. Each gram is slow to warm, thanks largely to hydrogen bonds. There is a huge mass of mixing water. And evaporation carries some heat away.
scenes.visual: Three icons line up under the Bay: a single BLUE gram block with GOLD dashes ('each gram slow to warm'), a deep layered block with mixing arrows ('huge mass, mixing'), and vapour wisps ('evaporation').
scenes.narration: So three things keep a bay steady. Each gram is slow to warm, thanks largely to hydrogen bonds. There is a huge mass of mixing water. And evaporation carries some heat away.

scenes.tts: So fish, crabs and grasses in the Bay face gentler daily swings than the air above them. A buoy in the Bay measured both, and the lesson shows what it recorded.
scenes.visual: Cartoon fish, a blue crab and swaying seagrass sit in calm BLUE water while a thermometer in the air above swings up and down. A yellow buoy bobs on the surface with one thermometer in the air and one in the water. No numbers are shown.
scenes.narration: So fish, crabs and grasses in the Bay face gentler daily swings than the air above them. A buoy in the Bay measured both, and the lesson shows what it recorded.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line on screen: 'Each gram of water warms slowly; a whole bay, slower still.'
